analysis.one_liner: Forces compulsory licensing of patented drugs a company keeps off the market when the public health needs them.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Jerrold Nadler's bill would let the Secretary of Health and Human Services flag patented drug-related products that are available to the public only in name — the company holds the patent but has not taken all reasonable steps to actually market the product, and the public's health depends on it. Once flagged, the Patent Office would be required to open the patent to compulsory licensing: other companies could use it after paying fees that get passed back to the patent holder. It applied to patents issued before, on, or after enactment. The bill never moved past referral to a Judiciary subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients whose health depends on a patented product a company has patented but not brought to market, and competing manufacturers who could enter and produce it.

how_it_helps.text: If the Secretary of Health and Human Services finds a patent holder has not taken all reasonable steps toward commercially marketing a product vital to public health, the Patent Office must provide for compulsory licensing of all patents relating to that product.
Licensees would pay fees set by the Commissioner, and those fees would be distributed back to the patent holders, so holders are compensated rather than stripped of the patent.
The bill applied to patents issued before, on, or after enactment, so it could reach existing shelved patents immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders, who would lose exclusive control over products they hold patents on but are not marketing, and who would receive only government-set fees in return.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharma patent holders of shelved products

drawbacks.text: Compulsory licensing reduces the value of holding a patent, which is the core reward for investing in drug development; critics of compulsory licensing generally argue it weakens the incentive to bring new products to market at all.

The trigger is vague: 'all reasonable steps toward commercial marketing' would be decided by the HHS Secretary, and companies could face losing exclusivity over business judgments a regulator later deems unreasonable.
The bill does not specify what the license fees would be — the Patent Office would set them by regulation, leaving patent holders' compensation uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Aimed at a real gap — patents held as blockers or shelved while the public waits for a needed product — and it preserved payment to holders rather than seizing patents outright. But the trigger standard is subjective, fees are left to regulation, and the incentive cost to future drug development is real. The bill got no cosponsors and no hearing, so no committee ever weighed those trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on introduction, sent to its intellectual property subcommittee a week later, and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Nadler introduced the bill on March 24, 1994, and it was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary the same day.
On March 31, 1994, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Intellectual Property and Judicial Administration.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors and no further action before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical patent holders, who keep exclusive control over patents they are not actively marketing, with no compulsory-licensing threat on the books.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharma patent holders keep shelved patents exclusive

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; it was his sole sponsorship effort with no cosponsors recruited.

against.name: House Committee on Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its intellectual property subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would open any patent on a vital-to-health product the holder is not marketing to compulsory licensing, ending exclusivity over shelved inventions in exchange for government-set fees. Patent exclusivity is the industry's core asset, and this bill directly limits how it can be used.
Compulsory licensing would let other manufacturers use shelved patented processes and products, creating entry opportunities where exclusivity currently blocks them.
